title: API 653 Training in Midland, TX: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 653 exam prep for Midland and Crane tank inspectors: crude terminal tanks, pipeline breakout tanks and tank batteries, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 653 Training in Midland: Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector Exam Prep for Midland and Crane Crude Terminals
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors at the Midland and Crane hubs

Crude produced across the Permian passes through tanks on its way out of the basin. RBN Energy has put crude storage at the Midland hub at roughly 20 million barrels and counted ten terminals at Crane, a smaller hub to the south, and pipelines such as ONEOK's Longhorn take crude from origin points at Crane, Barnhart and Midland toward Houston. Most of those terminal tanks are large, welded, atmospheric steel tanks, the kind API 653 was written for. This page is for the inspectors who look after them, and for tank battery and terminal staff who want to, who are preparing for the API 653 examination.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Midland. The API 653 course runs online and self-paced, with an instructor answering questions as you study, so it fits around terminal shifts and field rounds. API sets the eligibility rules in Annex D of API 653, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the certification. Atlantis does not hold API approval as a training provider, and the course itself confers no certification.

Terminal tanks at Midland and Crane

Terminal operators publish only part of what they hold, but what they do publish shows the size of the tanks. Sunoco LP lists a Midland South crude terminal that receives by pipeline and truck and delivers by pipeline, and its facility listings show tanks ranging from 55,000 to 255,000 barrels. Plains All American describes its Midland terminal as connected to all of its Permian joint venture gathering pipelines and to other terminals at the hub. Refinery tankage at Big Spring, where EIA lists the Delek-owned refinery at 73,000 barrels a day of crude capacity, sits up Interstate 20.

For an API 653 candidate, terminal tanks are the strongest preparation the basin offers. They are built to API 650, they go through the full cycle of out-of-service internal inspections, floor scans and repairs, and they generate the shell, bottom and settlement evaluations the examination asks about.

Tank batteries and other tanks that are not API 650 tanks

Most of the tanks a Midland field worker sees are not terminal tanks. Production sites hold crude, condensate and produced water in tank batteries, commonly built to API Specification 12F, which covers small shop-welded vertical tanks for production liquids, or to API 12D for larger field-welded ones. API 653 covers carbon and low-alloy steel tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor API 12C, welded or riveted, non-refrigerated and at atmospheric pressure, and older editions let an owner choose to apply it to other steel tanks built to a tank specification. That leaves several kinds of Permian storage outside its core scope:

  • Shop-welded production tanks. API 12F tanks are small and near atmospheric pressure; the 1994 edition of 12F gives standard sizes from 90 to 500 barrels, with a 750-barrel size in its table.
  • Non-metallic tanks. Fibreglass produced-water tanks, where a site uses them, fall outside a steel tank standard altogether.
  • Pressurised NGL storage. Bullets and spheres at gas plants and NGL facilities are pressure vessels. Where they serve a pipeline as breakout tanks built to API 2510, federal rules send their inspection to API 510.

Nothing stops an owner applying API 653 methods to production tanks. The exam, though, is written around API 650 tanks, so a candidate who has spent years on tank batteries has to learn API 650 construction details, from shell design and annular plates to nozzle reinforcement, that rarely come up in the field.

Two sets of spill rules: production sites and bulk storage

EPA's SPCC rule splits Midland's tanks in two, and the split decides whether an API 653 inspector is needed. At bulk storage facilities other than oil production sites, 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6) requires integrity testing of aboveground containers to an industry standard. EPA's fact sheet on the requirement says API 653 is typically used for field-erected tanks and that its formal external and internal inspections are carried out by an API 653 certified inspector, while STI SP001 is aimed at shop-built and small field-erected tanks. At onshore oil production facilities, 40 CFR 112.9(c)(3) asks instead for each container to be visually inspected on a regular schedule for deterioration and maintenance needs, including its foundation and supports.

So a crude terminal whose SPCC plan adopts API 653 needs certified inspectors for its formal inspections, while a tank battery usually does not. EPA requires test and inspection records to be kept for three years and recommends keeping formal reports for the life of the container. The SPCC integrity testing guide and the comparison of STI SP001 and API 653 go further.

Breakout tanks on the crude pipelines

A tank that relieves surges on a regulated hazardous liquid pipeline, or receives and stores crude for reinjection into it, is a breakout tank, and 49 CFR 195.432 governs it. Each in-service breakout tank must be inspected at least once each calendar year, at intervals not exceeding 15 months, and atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks must have their physical integrity inspected to API 653. The rule does not let API 653's risk-based method set the internal interval, so breakout tanks at Midland and Crane follow the standard interval rules. A PHMSA proposal published in June 2026 would relax that, within caps, but it had not become a final rule when this page was written. In Texas, the Railroad Commission oversees pipeline safety, breakout tanks included, for intrastate operators.

Bottoms, roofs and weather in West Texas

Dry air means less atmospheric corrosion on tank shells than on the Gulf Coast, and damage on Midland tanks concentrates where water gathers. Inside crude tanks, water and sediment settle on the floor, where corrosion under deposits and microbiologically influenced corrosion work on the plates and welds; concentration cell corrosion and MIC are both among the RP 571 sections the current API 653 Body of Knowledge tests. Underneath, the soil side of the floor depends on the pad, the drainage and the cathodic protection, which is why API RP 651 on cathodic protection and RP 652 on linings are part of the syllabus.

Weather still plays a part. Floating roofs, seals and roof drains have to cope with wind-blown dust and the occasional heavy downpour, and cold snaps make API 653's brittle fracture assessment worth learning thoroughly rather than skimming. The floating roof inspection guide and the floor pitting guide cover two of the commonest findings.

Worked example: a shell course on a Midland terminal tank

An exam-style shell evaluation on a tank of the size Midland terminals use. The tank is 150 ft in diameter with a maximum fill height of 48 ft, storing crude with a specific gravity of 0.85. The bottom course is A516 Grade 70 plate (yield 38,000 psi, tensile 70,000 psi), and the joint efficiency is 1.0.

  1. Allowable stress. For the bottom two courses API 653 uses the smaller of 0.80Y and 0.429T: 30,400 psi or 30,030 psi, so about 30,000 psi.
  2. Minimum thickness for the whole course. tmin = 2.6(H − 1)DG / SE = 2.6 × 47 × 150 × 0.85 / 30,000 = 0.519 in.
  3. A locally thinned area. For an area evaluated on its own, API 653 uses tmin = 2.6HDG / SE, with H measured from the bottom of the area up to the maximum liquid level. An area starting 9 ft above the floor uses H = 39 ft and needs only 0.431 in.
  4. Interval. The thinnest reading in the course is 0.735 in., and the corrosion rate N on the lower shell, where water and sediment sit, is 0.012 in. a year. The remaining corrosion allowance is 0.735 − 0.519 = 0.216 in. When the rate is known, API 653 sets the maximum ultrasonic shell thickness interval at the smaller of RCA/2N and 15 years: 0.216 / 0.024 = 9 years. With no known rate, the maximum would be five years.

Examiners like to change one variable at a time: a heavier product, a higher fill, a different plate. Working the same tank through those changes in practice questions is faster than learning each formula in isolation.

Routes into API 653 for Permian tank people

API's education and experience rules for this certification sit in Annex D of the standard and follow the same pattern as API 510 and 570, with tank experience gained in the last ten years while working for or under contract to an authorized inspection agency. The API 653 certification page has the detail. Typical Midland candidates come from:

  • Terminal operations and maintenance. Staff who have planned and witnessed tank work at Midland or Crane terminals know the tanks but need inspection experience on their record.
  • Tank construction and repair crews. Welders, fitters and QC staff from tank contractors bring construction and repair experience toward the longer routes.
  • NDT technicians. Floor scanning, UT thickness and vacuum box technicians who have worked under an API 653 inspector have hands-on inspection hours to describe.
  • Coating and cathodic protection specialists, whose knowledge of RP 651 and RP 652 covers part of the syllabus already.
  • Field production staff who have inspected tank batteries. Their tanks are usually not API 650 tanks, so describe the equipment accurately and let API decide how the experience counts.

Studying API 653 around terminal work

API 650 carries much of the open-book weight in the API 653 exam, and the current Body of Knowledge trims that load. It excludes a long list of API 650 annexes, among them D, E, F, J, K, L, P, T and W, along with the wind, seismic, venting and nozzle-load calculations, and it tests only sections 4.3.2 and 6.7 of RP 576. Knowing what is out lets a self-paced candidate spend the hours on what is in: shell and bottom evaluation, settlement, repairs and alterations, hydrotest decisions and the welding and NDE rules of Sections V and IX. Send the instructor the clause numbers of anything that will not reconcile, and the answer comes back with the reasoning that leads to it.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Midland or Crane terminal

A terminal with its own API 653 inspector can schedule formal external inspections and review contractor findings without waiting for an outside inspector's calendar, and a pipeline operator can keep its breakout tank records in experienced hands. Employers can enrol several candidates on one quote; fees are quoted on request. Give candidates the files for one or two of the terminal's own tanks to work alongside the course, so the shell, bottom and settlement exercises are about tanks they know.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 class in Midland or Odessa?
faq.a: There is no Atlantis classroom in Midland or Odessa. The API 653 course is self-paced online with instructor Q&A, so you can study from home or between terminal shifts. API administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres; once API accepts your application, Prometric's locator shows the centres closest to you. API issues the certification to candidates who pass.

faq.q: Do tank battery tanks need an API 653 inspector?
faq.a: Usually not under the federal spill rule. Onshore oil production facilities with an SPCC plan must visually inspect each container on a regular schedule, including its foundation and supports, rather than run the integrity testing programme required at bulk storage facilities. Battery tanks are also commonly built to API 12F or 12D rather than API 650. An owner may still choose API 653 methods, and its SPCC plan then governs.

faq.q: Does tank battery inspection count toward API 653 experience?
faq.a: API decides when it reviews your application. Annex D of API 653 asks for experience with tanks, gained while working for or under contract to an authorized inspection agency, and battery tanks are mostly built to production tank specifications rather than API 650. Describe the tanks, the work and your employer exactly. Terminal or refinery tank experience is the most direct fit for the code.

faq.q: Are the federal breakout tank rules on the API 653 exam?
faq.a: No. The Body of Knowledge lists API 653, API 650, the RP 571, 575, 576, 577, 651 and 652 recommended practices and ASME Sections V and IX. Regulations such as 49 CFR 195.432 and the SPCC rule are not examined. They still matter in Midland, because they decide which tanks need an API 653 inspector and how intervals are set.

faq.q: Which API 650 annexes can I leave out when studying for API 653?
faq.a: The current Body of Knowledge excludes Annexes D, E, F, J, K, L, P, SC, T, V, W, X and Y outright, and parts of G, I, M, O and S, keeping only their opening sections. It also excludes the wind, earthquake, nozzle-load, flange, venting and structural calculations. Check the list in the Body of Knowledge for your own window, because it can change.

faq.q: Is MIC on the API 653 exam?
faq.a: Yes. Microbiologically influenced corrosion is one of the RP 571 sections the current API 653 Body of Knowledge tests, alongside soil corrosion, concentration cell corrosion, brittle fracture, CUI, caustic and sulfuric acid corrosion and ethanol stress corrosion cracking. For a Midland inspector, MIC under the water and sediment on crude tank floors is one of the most practical of those to know well.

faq.q: Does an MFL floor scanning technician need API 653?
faq.a: No. Floor scanning is NDT, done by technicians qualified under their employer's written practice, and the API 653 inspector evaluates the results and decides on repairs. Many technicians later take API 653 to move into that role. Atlantis's ASNT SNT-TC-1A training covers MFL among other methods; the NDT training in Midland page describes it.

faq.q: Can a pipeline terminal enrol several tank inspectors together?
faq.a: Yes. Employers can enrol a group on one quote, and each candidate works through the self-paced course with access to the instructor. Candidates still apply to API one by one, and API checks each person's eligibility separately. Terminals often aim a group at the same exam window so candidates can work through practice papers together. Fees are quoted on request.
